name: Mid-size independent equipment leasing and finance company (Canada)
sector: financial services: commercial equipment leasing and finance
summary: This is a mid-size, privately owned independent equipment leasing and finance company in Canada, not modelled on any one firm. It leases and lends against commercial equipment such as trucks and trailers, construction and agricultural machinery, industrial and printing equipment, computers and office equipment, and medical and dental equipment, mostly to small and mid-sized businesses. About 54% of applications come from equipment dealers and manufacturers who offer its financing at the point of sale, about 32% from independent lease brokers and about 14% from its own account executives, who handle most of the larger mid-ticket deals. It funds about 1,400 contracts a month, roughly $925 million a year, and services about 55,000 active contracts with a net investment of about $1.5 billion. It earns the spread between lease and loan yields and its cost of funds, plus fees and residual gains, and funds itself by warehousing new contracts on a bank credit line and then selling pools of leases each month to bank-sponsored securitisation conduits. Its 340 staff sit in sales and origination, credit and risk, operations (documentation, funding, billing, customer service, insurance tracking and lease administration), collections and recoveries, asset management, finance, legal and compliance, internal audit, IT and HR, led from a head office in the Toronto area with sales staff across Canada.

evidence.note: Sum of the three channel drivers. Sized so that about 1,400 contracts fund each month (about 66% approved, about 62% of approvals funded), giving roughly $925 million a year, about 2.6% of the $35 billion Canadian equipment and commercial vehicle new business in 2019.

demand_drivers.name: Credit applications from vendor and dealer programs

evidence.note: Vendor share of about 54% of applications by count is an estimate for a small-ticket focused independent.
Broker share of about 32% by count is an estimate.
Direct share of about 14% by count, higher by dollars because direct deals are larger.

About 16,800 a year at an average of about $55,000 (small-ticket average about $36,000, mid-ticket about $380,000). The low end reflects the 2020 slowdown that CFLA expected (a 15% fall in equipment finance); the high end reflects the 2022 recovery, when the equipment and commercial vehicle market reached $42.2 billion.
Bookings of about 16,800 a year times an average life of about 3.3 years after prepayments. Net investment of about $1.5 billion, comparable to Chesswood's $1.7 billion group receivables.

About 5% of active contracts miss a payment date each month, mostly returned debits that cure within days; about 1.5% to 2.5% are over 30 days at any time, near the 2.3% ELFA reported for 2020. High end reflects the rise in 2020 that CFLA described.
About 70% of booked contracts run to term; the rest are paid out early.
About 0.2 contacts per active contract per month. CFLA's 2020 survey found 40% of members taking over 100 COVID-related calls a day, which sets the high end.
Estimate for a network of about 1,500 active dealers and 150 brokers with 15% to 20% annual churn.
Headcount of this organisation file; sets HR and IT volumes.

process_map.name: Onboard vendor and broker partners
process_map.description: A dealer or broker applies to join a program. Sales operations collects ownership, licences and banking details, credit support runs bureau and fraud checks on the business and its owners, legal approves any changes to the program agreement, and the partner is set up in the CRM and portal. Dealer fraud and incomplete paperwork make this slow.

evidence.note: Partner programs and vendor approvals are described in sources. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Design vendor and broker programs and rate cards
process_map.description: The director of vendor programs and pricing analysts set rates, terms, end-of-term options and fees for each program from cost of funds, residual tables and budget targets, then load rate cards to the portal. Each change needs approval from sales and finance and a system load, and dealers push for special rates.
process_map.unit_of_work: one program or rate card change

evidence.note: Vendor programs with set terms and end-of-term options are described. Volume is a tier C estimate.

process_map.name: Price non-standard and mid-ticket deals
process_map.description: Account executives and the vendor desk send deals that fall outside the rate card to the deal desk. A pricing analyst models yield, residual and cost of funds, and the sales operations manager or vice-president approves rates below the floor. Waiting for approval while a competitor quotes is the main delay.

evidence.note: Deal desk practice at mid-size lessors. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Provide point-of-sale payment quotes to dealers
process_map.description: A dealer calls, emails or uses the portal to ask what a customer's monthly payment would be. The vendor desk coordinator applies the program rate card, offers term and end-of-term options and, when the customer is ready, keys or uploads the credit application. Speed matters because the dealer is often with the customer.

evidence.note: Point-of-sale vendor financing is described. Quote volume of about two quotes per vendor application is a tier C estimate.

process_map.name: Review dealer program performance
process_map.description: Vendor account managers and regional managers review each active dealer's volume, approval and booking rates, delinquency and any fraud or documentation problems, using portfolio reports. Poor performers get training, restricted programs or termination. Data by dealer often needs manual cleaning.

evidence.note: Partner scorecards are a common control in vendor finance. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Manage the broker panel
process_map.description: The broker channel manager and relationship managers review each broker's submissions, approval rates, early defaults and fraud flags, adjust commission and buy rates and remove brokers whose deals perform badly. Brokers send the same deal to several lessors, so look-to-book rates are low.

evidence.note: Estimate based on common broker channel management. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Originate and structure direct deals
process_map.description: Account executives find and meet established businesses, gather equipment quotes and financial statements, structure the lease or loan (term, residual, seasonal payments) and submit the application. Larger deals need equipment valuations and deal desk pricing before submission.

evidence.note: Direct mid-ticket sales common among independents serving SMEs. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Communicate credit decisions and negotiate conditions
process_map.description: Vendor desk, broker desk and account executives tell the dealer, broker or customer the decision and any conditions such as a larger down payment, guarantee or shorter term. They negotiate counter-offers, send appeals back to credit and, once the customer accepts, ask documentation to prepare contracts.

evidence.note: Broker liaison on approvals and documents is described in the posting. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Calculate sales commissions
process_map.description: Each month the CRM administrator pulls funded volume and margin by salesperson, applies the incentive plan, resolves disputes about deal credit and sends approved statements to payroll. Plan exceptions and split credits cause manual work.

evidence.note: Standard monthly incentive process; estimate.

process_map.name: Receive and set up credit applications
process_map.description: Applications arrive through the portal, email and the broker desk inbox. A credit coordinator checks they are complete, matches the customer to existing exposure, pulls commercial and personal bureau reports, runs preliminary checks and routes the file to small-ticket or mid-ticket credit or to fraud review. Missing information is the most common delay.

evidence.note: Intake duties from the credit coordinator posting. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Verify identity and investigate fraud flags
process_map.description: Applications, funding packages and new partners flagged for mismatched identity, inflated invoices, unknown dealers or altered documents go to a fraud analyst. The analyst checks corporate registries, calls the dealer and customer, confirms serial numbers and clears or declines the file.

evidence.note: Posting lists corporate and land registry checks and escalation of unusual items. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Adjudicate small-ticket credit applications
process_map.description: For applications up to $250,000 the scoring engine grades the bureau and application data. A credit analyst reviews the result, checks time in business, guarantor credit and equipment type, and approves, declines or counter-offers within delegated limits. Files above an analyst's limit go to a senior analyst or manager.

evidence.note: Adjudication within policy with escalation is described. Share of about 87% of applications under $250,000 and the scoring engine are tier C estimates.

process_map.name: Underwrite mid-ticket credit applications
process_map.description: Applications above $250,000 get a full credit memo: financial statement spreading, cash flow coverage, industry and management review, guarantor strength and equipment valuation. Senior analysts recommend a structure and send the memo for approval at the right level. Waiting for financial statements and valuations stretches the cycle to days.

evidence.note: Mid-ticket underwriting practice. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Approve credit above delegated authority
process_map.description: Credit memos above an analyst's or manager's limit go to the director of credit, the chief credit and risk officer or the credit committee for the largest exposures. Approvers question the structure, add conditions or decline. Approver availability is the main wait.

evidence.note: Delegated authority structure common at lessors. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Review large customer exposures annually
process_map.description: Customers with total exposure above about $500,000 or on the watch list get an annual review. A senior analyst collects new financial statements, checks payment history and covenants and updates the risk rating, which feeds portfolio monitoring. Chasing customers for statements takes weeks.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Monitor portfolio credit risk
process_map.description: Portfolio analysts build the monthly risk report: delinquency and losses by channel, vintage, industry, region and dealer, concentrations, restructures and watch list. The report goes to credit policy, partner reviews, lenders, accounting for loss allowances and the board.

evidence.note: Delinquency and loss measures are the industry's standard indicators.

process_map.name: Maintain credit policy and scorecards
process_map.description: The credit policy manager reviews performance against policy, adjusts scorecard cut-offs, industry limits and delegated authorities, gets approval from the chief credit and risk officer or the board, and asks IT to change the decision engine.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage enterprise risk
process_map.description: Each quarter the enterprise risk analyst updates the risk register and appetite measures with credit, funding, operational, compliance and cyber risks, using audit, compliance and security reports, and prepares the risk committee report.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Prepare lease and loan documents
process_map.description: A documentation specialist generates the master lease or loan agreement, schedule, guarantee, pre-authorised debit form and delivery and acceptance certificate from the approval, adds approval conditions and sends the package for electronic or wet signature. Quebec contracts need French versions, and non-standard wording goes to legal. Changes to equipment or price after the documents are sent cause rework.

evidence.note: Document preparation is described in sources. About 2,000 packages for 1,400 fundings is a tier C estimate.

process_map.name: Search registries and register security interests
process_map.description: Registration clerks search the provincial personal property registry or Quebec's RDPRM for the customer and serial numbers, then register a financing statement or publish the lease and file the verification. Leases over one year must be registered or published to protect the company against third parties, and timing matters for priority.

evidence.note: Registration rules from the BC PPSA and Quebec Civil Code article 1852. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Audit signed packages and fund vendors
process_map.description: A funding specialist checks the signed package against the approval: signatures, guarantees, the vendor invoice and serial numbers, registration, insurance evidence and a delivery and acceptance call to the customer. Exceptions go back to sales or credit, and cleared files are approved for vendor payment. Missing or wrong documents are the main cause of rework.

evidence.note: Funding review and credit audit are described. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Book contracts and set up billing
process_map.description: The funding specialist sets the contract up in the lease system: payment schedule, tax jurisdiction and codes, asset records, accounting classification and insurance requirement, then sends a welcome package. A billing specialist checks a sample. Wrong tax codes or dates found later cause rebills.

evidence.note: Standard booking step in lease operations. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Track equipment insurance
process_map.description: Coordinators record certificates naming the company as loss payee, check coverage and expiry dates, send letters when insurance lapses and enrol uninsured customers in the protection program, which adds a monthly charge. Certificates that list the wrong insured or omit equipment are common.

evidence.note: Insurance clauses requiring loss payee status are standard in equipment leases. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Run daily billing and debit files
process_map.description: Each business day the lease system produces invoices for contracts due, adds GST/HST, QST or PST by province and fees, and builds the pre-authorised debit file. Billing specialists review exceptions, apply amendments and adjustments, release the debit file to the bank and post the billing to the ledger. About 55,000 contracts are billed each month.
process_map.unit_of_work: one daily billing run with its exceptions

evidence.note: Daily billing cycle is an assumption; lessors must collect provincial sales tax on lease payments.

process_map.name: Apply customer payments
process_map.description: Most payments arrive by pre-authorised debit and post automatically. Clerks apply the rest: cheques from the lockbox, EFT and wires with unclear references, partial payments and payments for several contracts, and clear unapplied cash. Daily totals go to treasury, funders and the ledger.
process_map.unit_of_work: one payment item needing manual application

evidence.note: Assumes about 85% of payments by pre-authorised debit. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Process returned debits
process_map.description: The bank returns debits for insufficient funds, stopped payments and closed accounts. A clerk reverses the payment, adds the returned payment fee and places the account in the early collections queue the same day.

evidence.note: About 2.5% of debits returned in a normal month; the high end reflects the 2020 rise in delinquency.

process_map.name: Handle customer, dealer and broker service requests
process_map.description: Representatives answer calls and emails about invoices, payment dates, copies of contracts, address and banking changes, insurance and payouts. They resolve simple requests on the call and route payouts, assumptions, restructures, complaints and casualty losses to the right team. Call peaks follow billing dates.

evidence.note: Customer support is part of the servicing life cycle. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Quote and process early buyouts
process_map.description: A lease administration specialist calculates the payout (remaining payments discounted per the contract, residual or purchase option and taxes), sends the quote and, when paid, terminates billing, notifies treasury if the contract was sold to a conduit and requests title transfer. Dealer trade-ups need quick quotes.

evidence.note: About 1.5% of active contracts request a payout quote each month and about 40% complete. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Transfer leases to new lessees
process_map.description: When a customer sells its business or equipment, the buyer may take over the lease. The new lessee goes through credit, lease administration prepares an assumption agreement, registrations are amended and billing is moved. The original lessee is released only if credit agrees.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Restructure and defer payments
process_map.description: Customers in difficulty, referred by service or collections, ask to defer payments or extend the term. A senior credit analyst approves the change, lease administration documents and rebooks it, and treasury reports the modification to funders. In 2020 many lessors handled waves of COVID deferral requests.

evidence.note: Deferral surveys in 2020 are documented; the high value is the 2020 peak. Mode is tier C.

process_map.name: Manage end of term
process_map.description: About 60 to 90 days before expiry the lease system lists maturing contracts and a notice of options goes to the customer: buy at the stated option or fair market value, renew, return or upgrade. Specialists price fair market value purchases with asset management, process elections, start month-to-month billing when the customer does not reply and arrange returns.

evidence.note: End-of-lease options and notice timing described by a Canadian lender. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Transfer title and discharge registrations
process_map.description: After a payout, purchase option, casualty settlement or remarketing sale, a specialist issues a bill of sale and a registration clerk discharges the PPSA or RDPRM registration. Customers and their banks chase late discharges.

evidence.note: Registration and discharge under PPSA. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Settle casualty losses
process_map.description: When leased equipment is destroyed or stolen, the specialist calculates the stipulated loss value, files or follows the insurance claim with the insurance team, applies the insurer's payment and closes the contract.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Collect early-stage delinquencies
process_map.description: Collectors work queues of accounts 1 to 30 days late, call and email customers, take promises to pay, re-run debits and refer customers who cannot pay to restructuring. Most accounts cure within two weeks.

evidence.note: Industry delinquency of about 2.3% over 30 days used to size flows. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Collect late-stage delinquencies
process_map.description: Accounts more than 30 days late move to senior collectors who contact owners and guarantors, issue default notices, negotiate settlements and recommend repossession or write-off. Each file needs judgement on the customer's prospects and the equipment's value.

evidence.note: About 24% of newly delinquent accounts pass 30 days. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Repossess equipment
process_map.description: A recovery officer confirms the registration and default, instructs a bailiff, tracks the seizure, arranges transport and storage and sends the required notice of intended disposition to the customer and guarantors.

evidence.note: Seizure and disposition rules in PPSA. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Recover deficiencies and approve write-offs
process_map.description: After sale proceeds are applied, the recovery officer pursues the remaining balance from the customer and guarantors, places files with agencies or lawyers and recommends write-off. Write-offs need approval from the director or the chief credit and risk officer and are reported to funders.

evidence.note: About 70 write-offs a month at about $16,000 net gives losses near 0.9% of receivables, above ELFA's 0.48% all-size average because of the small-ticket mix.

process_map.name: Value equipment and set residuals
process_map.description: Asset managers value equipment for mid-ticket deals, used equipment and fair market value options, order third-party inspections when needed and maintain residual tables by equipment type and term.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Recover off-lease equipment
process_map.description: When a customer returns equipment at end of term, coordinators book transport to a storage yard, get a condition report and bill excess wear or missing parts.

evidence.note: About 7% of maturing contracts return equipment. Volume is a tier C estimate derived from the demand driver.

process_map.name: Remarket repossessed and returned equipment
process_map.description: Remarketing specialists choose a channel (auction, dealer, online listing or direct buyer), set reserve prices, arrange repairs and sell the equipment, then apply the proceeds and issue the bill of sale.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Select and sell securitisation pools
process_map.description: Each month a securitisation analyst selects eligible new contracts against each conduit's criteria and concentration limits, builds the data tape and schedule, calculates the advance and reserves and settles the sale. Conduit funding pays down the bank line used to warehouse new contracts.
process_map.unit_of_work: one pool sale to a conduit

evidence.note: Bank-sponsored conduits buying equipment lease pools are documented. Three conduit facilities is a tier C estimate.

process_map.name: Prepare servicer reports for funders
process_map.description: Analysts reconcile collections, payouts, modifications and defaults for each securitised pool, calculate triggers and reserves and send the monthly servicer report and data file to each conduit.

evidence.note: Monthly reporting on conduit assets is described; conduit transactions backed by Canadian equipment leases are rated under a dedicated methodology.

process_map.name: Report borrowing base and covenants to banks
process_map.description: Treasury calculates the monthly borrowing base of eligible receivables and the quarterly covenant ratios, and the chief financial officer signs the compliance certificate for the bank syndicate.
process_map.unit_of_work: one borrowing base or compliance report

evidence.note: Revolving bank syndicate funding at a Canadian lessor is documented; reporting cadence is tier C.

process_map.name: Manage daily cash and release payments
process_map.description: Each morning the treasury analyst reviews cash, collections and the funding queue, draws on the credit line if needed and releases approved vendor and broker payments by EFT.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage interest rate and funding risk
process_map.description: Each month the treasurer compares fixed-rate lease cash flows with floating-rate bank and conduit funding, reviews interest rate hedges and remaining funding capacity, and updates the cost of funds that pricing uses. Rate moves between approval and funding squeeze margins.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Close the books each month
process_map.description: Accountants reconcile the lease subledger, cash, securitisation balances and suppliers to the general ledger, post accruals and the loss allowance and produce monthly financial statements within about eight business days.

evidence.note: Standard monthly close; timing estimate.

process_map.name: Account for leases and expected credit losses
process_map.description: Lease accountants check the IFRS 16 classification of new contracts, review residual values, calculate finance income and the IFRS 9 expected credit loss allowance using portfolio risk data, and post the entries.

evidence.note: Lessor accounting requirements described by BDO; IFRS 16 effective 2019.

process_map.name: Pay operating suppliers
process_map.description: Clerks match and code supplier invoices for rent, software, bailiffs, storage, legal and registry fees, route them for approval under the signing authority policy and pay them in weekly runs. Bailiff and storage invoices must be charged back to customer accounts.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Complete the annual audit
process_map.description: After year end the controller's team prepares schedules and evidence for the external auditor, answers questions on allowances, residuals and securitisation, and issues audited statements to the board, banks and conduits.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: File sales tax returns
process_map.description: Sales tax analysts reconcile tax billed and collected by province from billing, buyouts and asset sales, prepare GST/HST, QST and BC, Saskatchewan and Manitoba returns and remit the tax.

evidence.note: BC lessors must register and collect PST. Number of returns is tier C.

process_map.name: Prepare income tax and capital cost allowance
process_map.description: The tax accountant groups leased assets by capital cost allowance class, applies the specified leasing property rules to non-exempt assets, prepares quarterly tax provisions and instalments and files federal and Quebec corporate returns with the auditors' review.
process_map.unit_of_work: one quarterly provision or annual return

evidence.note: CCA classes and the specified leasing property split are documented.

process_map.name: Handle property tax assessments
process_map.description: A few assessments arrive each month, mainly on leased equipment at designated industrial sites in Alberta. The analyst checks the assessment, pays or appeals it and rebills the lessee under the contract.

evidence.note: Most Canadian provinces do not tax movable equipment, so volume is small; Alberta assesses designated industrial property annually.

process_map.name: Budget and forecast
process_map.description: The planning team builds the annual budget and quarterly reforecasts of originations, margins, losses, funding and headcount with each executive, and the board approves the budget.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Produce monthly management reporting
process_map.description: After the close, planning analysts combine financial results, origination volumes by channel, approval rates, portfolio delinquency and operating metrics into the monthly management report, and collect variance explanations from each executive.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage legal actions and insolvency claims
process_map.description: Legal counsel and paralegals manage court actions against customers and guarantors, file proofs of claim with trustees, defend the company's ownership in insolvencies and instruct external lawyers.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Maintain contract templates and review legal terms
process_map.description: Legal counsel maintains lease, loan, guarantee and partner agreement templates in English and French, reviews non-standard terms that customers, dealers and brokers ask for, and advises documentation on unusual security or multi-province situations.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Handle complaints and monitor compliance
process_map.description: Compliance analysts log and investigate complaints, answer privacy access requests, track training attestations and test controls such as French-language contract rules and anti-spam consent, and report results.
process_map.unit_of_work: one complaint, request or monitoring test

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Perform internal audits
process_map.description: Internal audit runs a risk-based plan of about twelve audits a year (funding, collections, securitisation, access, close), tests controls and reports findings and action plans to the audit committee.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Report to the board
process_map.description: The executive office assembles quarterly board and committee packs from management, risk, audit, compliance and financial reports, records decisions and passes board direction to management.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Recruit and onboard staff
process_map.description: Recruiters post approved roles, screen candidates, coordinate interviews and offers and set up new hires for payroll, system access and training. Collections and customer service turnover drives most hiring.

evidence.note: About 15% annual turnover plus growth.

process_map.name: Run payroll and benefits
process_map.description: Payroll specialists collect hires, leavers, changes and commission statements, process bi-weekly pay and deductions, send the file to the payroll provider, reconcile government remittances and send the cost journal to accounting.

evidence.note: Bi-weekly payroll plus off-cycle runs.

process_map.name: Manage performance and training
process_map.description: HR runs annual performance reviews, onboarding training for new collectors and service staff, required compliance and privacy training and industry courses, and keeps training records that compliance uses for attestations.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Provision and review system access
process_map.description: Security and service desk staff grant, change and remove access to the lease system, portals and bank portal from approved requests and run quarterly access reviews with managers.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage system changes and releases
process_map.description: Business analysts and developers specify, build and test changes to the lease system, partner portal, decision engine rules, rate tables and integrations, and release them after business sign-off. Testing billing and tax changes is the slowest part.

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Resolve IT service requests
process_map.description: Service desk analysts log incidents and requests from staff, such as password resets, printer and phone problems and lease system errors, fix what they can and escalate problems that need code or configuration changes.

evidence.note: About 1.75 tickets per employee per month.

process_map.name: Maintain the data warehouse and reports
process_map.description: Each night data loads from the lease system, collections and payments into the warehouse. Data developers fix failed loads and maintain the reports used by risk, treasury and planning.
process_map.unit_of_work: one daily data load and report cycle

evidence.note: Estimate.

process_map.name: Manage information security and disaster recovery
process_map.description: Security staff patch and scan systems after supplier advisories, monitor alerts, handle incidents such as phishing and account compromise, run disaster recovery tests of the lease system and report results to risk management.

evidence.note: Estimate.

assumptions: Scale was chosen, not observed: about 1,400 fundings a month, 55,000 active contracts, $1.5 billion net investment and 340 staff. Ratios between these were checked against Chesswood and CWB disclosures but no single company was copied.
Channel mix by application count is about 54% vendor and dealer, 32% broker and 14% direct; by dollars direct and broker mid-ticket deals weigh more. These shares are estimates.
Small-ticket means up to $250,000 and is about 87% of applications. Average funded amount is about $36,000 for small-ticket and about $380,000 for mid-ticket.

About 66% of decided applications are approved and about 62% of approvals fund, because dealers and brokers shop deals to several lessors. These ratios are estimates; the ELFA survey tracks approval ratios but the figures were not available to cite.
Delinquency and losses are sized from ELFA's 2020 US figures (2.3% over 30 days, 0.48% net losses) adjusted upward for a small-ticket independent; Canadian lessor-level figures could not be sourced.
Loaded cost per hour is 2019-2022 wage times 1.35. 2019-2022 wages were taken as about 90% of Job Bank 2023-2024 Ontario figures, because Job Bank shows only current survey periods.
About 85% of customers pay by pre-authorised debit. Billing is modelled as one daily run with exceptions, not as single invoices.

Funding: new contracts are warehoused on a syndicated bank revolving facility and sold monthly to three bank-sponsored ABCP conduits. Some independents also used BDC's F-PIL platform described by CFLA; it is treated as one of the conduits.
Contracts sold to conduits stay on the balance sheet, as CWB's note 8 describes for its own securitisations, so accounting books a securitisation liability.

Property tax on movable equipment is minor in Canada; the process covers occasional assessments such as Alberta designated industrial property. Personal property tax compliance of the kind US lessors run is out of scope.
Non-bank lessors had no prudential regulator and were not FINTRAC reporting entities in 2019-2022; identity and fraud checks are done for credit and fraud reasons.
High ends of volume ranges reflect 2020: CFLA reported surging COVID calls and payment deferral requests and a rise in delinquency to levels like 2009-10.
Ranges for cases per month on annual or quarterly processes are expressed as fractions (0.08 is one a year, 0.33 is one a quarter).

Some functions are outsourced: bailiffs, auctions, transport and storage, registry filings through service firms, external collections and law firms, payroll processing and the protection program insurer.
Job postings used as evidence are from after 2022; the roles they describe existed in the reference period, but pay was adjusted.
